messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur is a 78-year-old divorced man who works as a database administrator, a job he has held for over three decades. He sought help after his primary care physician referred him, concerned about his escalating anxiety and social withdrawal. The event that shattered his sense of safety occurred two years ago, when a routine hospital stay for a minor infection spiraled into septic shock. For three days, Arthur lay in the ICU, tethered to machines, the sterile antiseptic smell of the ward and the acrid tang of his own failing body filling his nostrils. He remembers the stark fluorescent lights, the beeping monitors, and the suffocating certainty that he was dying alone. That smell—the sharp, chemical scent of the ICU—returns to him unbidden now, often when he least expects it, and when it does, the memory feels more real and vivid than the room he is actually standing in. He will be at his desk, running a database query, and suddenly he is back in that bed, the sheets rough against his skin, the fear as fresh as it was then. The memory does not just replay; it overtakes him, and he has come to believe that this is proof that his body has turned against him, that it cannot be trusted to stay calm even when he is safe at home.

Arthur’s home, once his sanctuary, now feels like another battleground. He is hypervigilant there, scanning for any sign of physical decline—a twinge in his chest, a slight cough—convinced that his body is a ticking time bomb that will betray him again. This constant state of alert has eroded his faith in the world. He is certain that the world is a dangerous place, full of invisible threats, and that his own body is the most treacherous of all. What frightens him most is the way this threat feels has reshaped his entire outlook: he has lost his faith in people, in life, and in any higher power. He used to be a man of quiet routines, but now he sees every minor ache as a prelude to catastrophe. The hypervigilance feeds directly into this bleak appraisal, because every moment of being on guard reinforces his belief that danger is everywhere and that he is fundamentally unsafe.

Over the months, Arthur’s avoidance has become a cage. He stopped visiting his adult children, afraid that any excitement or stress might trigger a medical crisis. He stopped going to the grocery store, ordering everything online, because the crowds felt like a vector for infection. His job, once a source of stability, is now a daily trial: he works from home, but the very act of sitting at his computer reminds him of the hours he spent in the ICU, waiting for test results. He has come to believe that his memory of the event is a kind of curse, that the vivid reliving is a sign that his body is still fighting a war it already lost. The connection between the intrusive memories and his negative appraisals is tight: every time the olfactory recall hits, he thinks, *See? My body is still reacting. I am still in danger.* And every time he feels that threat, he reaffirms his belief that the world is hostile and his own flesh is an enemy.

What finally brought Arthur to therapy was a concrete consequence: he nearly lost his job. His hypervigilance had made him so distractible that he missed a critical system update, causing a data outage. His supervisor, a younger woman who did not know about his hospitalization, put him on a performance improvement plan. Arthur was terrified—not of losing the job, but of what it would mean: that he could no longer function, that the world had truly become too dangerous for him to navigate. He is most afraid that therapy will confirm his worst fear—that his body is broken and his mind is following suit—but he is also, quietly, hoping that someone can show him a way out of the loop. He wants to believe, again, that he can sit in his own living room without feeling like he is back in that ICU bed, that he can smell coffee instead of antiseptic, and that he can trust his own heart to keep beating without his constant vigilance.
